canonical_topic: Three storage facility types and their cushion-gas requirements
definition: Natural gas storage is built in one of three geological settings — depleted gas reservoirs, salt caverns, or aquifers — each with a distinct cost, performance, and required cushion-gas profile.
core_idea: Depleted reservoirs are the cheapest and most common option; salt caverns cost more to develop but deliver much higher performance (higher pressure tolerance, faster cycling); aquifers are used only where neither alternative is available and are the least efficient of the three.
key_points: Depleted gas reservoirs: cheapest, most reliable, most historically abundant; require reserving about 50% of capacity as cushion gas.
Salt caverns: more expensive to build but highest performance (least leakage, strongest walls, highest pressure tolerance, most frequent cycling); require reserving about 33% of capacity as cushion.
Aquifers: used only when neither depleted reservoirs nor salt caverns are available; least desirable performance; require reserving about 80% of capacity as cushion.
Cushion gas is the portion of a facility's total capacity that must stay in place (working gas is the remainder available for injection/withdrawal cycles).
relationships: Cushion-gas ratios explain why salt caverns are preferred for high-cycling, price-sensitive strategies despite higher build cost.
Ties to the maximum-pressure concept: salt caverns' superior pressure tolerance is the source of their performance edge.
trading_implications: A facility's cushion-gas ratio directly limits how much working (tradeable) gas volume it actually offers, which matters when valuing or leasing storage capacity.
Salt caverns' faster cycling ability makes them better suited to capturing frequent, erratic price swings than depleted reservoirs or aquifers.
caveats: Assuming a facility's nameplate capacity is all usable working gas — a large fraction is permanently reserved as cushion gas and never available for trading cycles.
